newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO still seeking peace - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO still seeking peace - analysts.

text.p: Violence raged in the West Bank and Gaza this week but Palestinian and Israeli analysts said peace efforts were far from dead.

They said Israeli and PLO officials were holding informal and secret contacts to find a way out of a crisis that has paralysed peace talks for more than three months, since Israel began work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"I believe that both sides are making calculated confrontations with defined red lines for each side while on the political level, it seems there are efforts to find a way out of the crisis," said Ghassan al-Khatib, a former Palestinian negotiator.
Israeli officials, who declined to be identified, said there was a lot of movement below the surface on the peace process despite the apparent failure of U.S. and Egyptian mediation efforts.

One meeting was between Mahmoud Abbas, better known as Abu Mazen, a top Palestine Liberation Organisation official and an architect of the 1993 Israel-PLO self-rule deal, and Israel's National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon.
The second meeting was between the head of Israel's security liaison committee Herzl Getz and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

"There are events that are taking place...the meeting between Arafat and Getz. There are a series of meetings taking place at the working level," said Gerald Steinberg, of the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies at Israel's Bar-Ilan university.
Palestinan officials said the meeting was exploratory and informal.

"We and the Israelis constantly carry out mutual explorations of positions. This struggle is in the framework of negotiations," Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, general secretary of the Palestinian Authority told a news conference earlier this week, referring to the Abbas-Sharon meeting.

Steinberg said he believed efforts were focused on finding a framework for talks on a permanent peace settlement and the second phase of an Israeli redeployment from mostly rural areas in the West Bank.
"I think the real focus is on the final status framework and the interim withdrawal that is scheduled to take place in September," he said.

Israel said after the meeting that security coordination between the two side, severed since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu sent bulldozers to start working on the Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem in March, had been restored.
Palestinians denied it, insisting that resumption of full security cooperation was linked to freezing settlement-building in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"A key component for Israel is that security cooperation shouldn't be used as a negotiating tool but should continue on a constant basis," one Israeli official said.

The contacts were taking place as Israeli soldiers and Palestinians squared off in a week of clashes across the invisible line that divides the West Bank town of Hebron into two sections, one controlled by Israel and the other by the PLO.
Soldiers resorted to live ammunition and unleashed undercover units posing as Palestinians to fight Arabs who rained stones and petrol bombs on them.
Palestinians say the violence was a spontaneous reflection of the frustrations they have felt since Israel began building the settlement at Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa.

Tensions rose further after the discovery on Hebron storefronts on Saturday of anti-Moslem hate posters depicting the Prophet Mohammad as a pig. Israeli police said a Jewish woman, now under arrest, was responsible.
Analysts on both sides said they believed there was a tacit understanding to keep the violence under control so as to let out steam on the Palestinian side falling short of an all-out explosion.
The analysts noted the confrontations were confined to Hebron and small pockets in Gaza.
"It is part of the push and pull of the negotiating process. The danger is for an extremist to light a match," Steinberg said.
